issues.title: [inductor] TypeVar(default=) breaks Python 3.11: torch._inductor fails to import on Python < 3.13 (regression in 2.10.0)
issues.author: swagglian
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## 🐛 Bug Report

### Summary

`torch 2.10.0` uses `TypeVar(default=...)` (introduced in [PEP 696](https://peps.python.org/pep-0696/)) in `torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py`, but this syntax is only natively supported in Python 3.13+. On Python 3.11, it raises a `TypeError` at import time, making the entire `torch._inductor` module unusable.

This was initially reported in #187241, which was closed as "cannot reproduce" — but the root cause is Python version specific and was not tested on Python 3.11.

---

### Error Message

```
TypeError: TypeVar.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'default'
```

Full traceback when importing `torch._inductor`:

```
File ".../torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py", line 77, in CuteDSLSubgraphInfo
    cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None
         ~~~^^^^^
TypeError: Too few arguments for <class 'torch._inductor.codegen.common.CSE'>; actual 1, expected 2
```

---

### Minimal Reproduction

```python
# Reproduces on Python 3.11, works on Python 3.13+
from typing import TypeVar
AugmentedKeyT = TypeVar("AugmentedKeyT", default=str)
```

Output on Python 3.11:
```
TypeError: TypeVar.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'default'
```

Also reproduces via import:
```bash
python3 -c "from torch._inductor.codegen.cutedsl.cutedsl_kernel import CuteDSLTemplateKernel"
```

---

### Root Cause

In `torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py`:

```python
AugmentedKeyT = TypeVar("AugmentedKeyT", default=str)

class CSE(Generic[CSEVariableType, AugmentedKeyT]):
    ...
```

`TypeVar(default=...)` is a Python 3.13+ feature ([PEP 696](https://peps.python.org/pep-0696/)). On Python 3.11:
- `TypeVar` does not accept the `default` keyword argument → `TypeError`
- Even if ignored, `AugmentedKeyT` has no default, so `CSE[Any]` (one argument) is invalid for `CSE(Generic[CSEVariableType, AugmentedKeyT])` (two parameters) → second `TypeError`

This makes the entire inductor import chain fail on Python 3.11.

---

### Environment

- PyTorch version: `2.10.0+cpu`
- Python version: `3.11.4`
- OS: openEuler (aarch64)
- Install: `torch-2.10.0+cpu-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl` (official wheel)

---

### Expected Behavior

`torch._inductor` imports successfully on Python 3.11, which is still a supported version for torch 2.10.0.

---

### Suggested Fix

Option 1 — Use `typing_extensions` for backport support:
```python
from typing_extensions import TypeVar
AugmentedKeyT = TypeVar("AugmentedKeyT", default=str)
```

Option 2 — Version guard:
```python
import sys
if sys.version_info >= (3, 13):
    from typing import TypeVar as TypeVar313
    AugmentedKeyT = TypeVar313("AugmentedKeyT", default=str)
else:
    AugmentedKeyT = TypeVar("AugmentedKeyT")
```

Option 3 — Update `cutedsl_kernel.py` to use two explicit type arguments:
```python
# Before
cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None

# After
cse: Optional[CSE[Any, Any]] = None
```

---

### Related

- Closes #187241 (previously closed as cannot reproduce, root cause was Python version)
- PEP 696: https://peps.python.org/pep-0696/

### Versions

orch-2.10.0+cpu-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl

issues.title: [inductor] TypeError: Too few arguments for CSE in cutedsl_kernel.py (torch 2.10.0, Python 3.11)
issues.author: swagglian
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Bug Report

### Summary

In `torch 2.10.0`, `torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py` references `CSE[Any]` with only one type argument, but the `CSE` class in `torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py` is defined as `Generic[CSEVariableType, AugmentedKeyT]`, which requires two type arguments. This causes a `TypeError` at import time on Python 3.11.

### Error Message

```
TypeError: Too few arguments for <class 'torch._inductor.codegen.common.CSE'>; actual 1, expected 2
```

Full traceback:
```
File ".../torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py", line 77, in CuteDSLSubgraphInfo
    cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None
         ~~~^^^^^
TypeError: Too few arguments for <class 'torch._inductor.codegen.common.CSE'>; actual 1, expected 2
```

### Root Cause

In `torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py`, the `CSE` class is defined with two generic parameters:

```python
# torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py, line 1886
class CSE(Generic[CSEVariableType, AugmentedKeyT]):
```

However, in `torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py`, it is used with only one type argument:

```python
# torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py, line 77
cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None
```

This internal inconsistency was introduced when `CSE` was refactored to accept a second generic parameter, but `cutedsl_kernel.py` was not updated accordingly.

Note: On Python 3.11, both `Optional[CSE[Any]]` and `CSE[Any] | None` trigger runtime generic type validation, so changing the annotation syntax alone does not fix the issue. The correct fix is:

```python
cse: Optional[CSE[Any, Any]] = None
```

### Steps to Reproduce

```bash
python3 -c "from torch._inductor.codegen.cutedsl.cutedsl_kernel import CuteDSLTemplateKernel"
```

### Environment

- PyTorch version: 2.10.0+cpu
- Python version: 3.11.4
- OS: openEuler (aarch64)
- Install source: official wheel `torch-2.10.0+cpu-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl`

### Expected Behavior

The module imports successfully without any `TypeError`.

### Suggested Fix

In `torch/_inductor/codegen/cutedsl/cutedsl_kernel.py`, update the annotation:

```python
# Before
cse: Optional[CSE[Any]] = None

# After
cse: Optional[CSE[Any, Any]] = None
```

### Versions

https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu/torch-2.10.0%2Bcpu-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl

Hi @jansel,

The issue is specific to Python 3.11. The root cause is:

Workaround on Python 3.11: change `CSE[Any]` to `CSE[Any, Any]` in cutedsl_kernel.py.

issues.title: [RFC] support symmetric memory in torch.compile
issues.author: zou3519
issues.body:
The proposal originally came up in vLLM-compile sync with @ProExpertProg, @Chillee, and @Amir-19 and was also discussed with @ngimel @kwen2501. Recording it here to make sure we're all on the same page.

## Pitch

For any collective operator (built-in or custom), a user can specify which input must have symmetric memory.

torch.compile (Inductor) will figure out where the input is coming from and ensure that it is allocated with symmetric memory.

There are two cases for what type of operator produced the input.

1) built-in operator. Inductor might already preallocate the buffer that is the output of the operator (via memory planning) and it just needs to allocate it with symmetric memory.

```py
requires_symmetric_memory(collective, input=0)

def user_code(x):
    y = x.sin()
    z = y.cos()
    return collective(z)

def inductor_generated_code(x):
    with symmetric_memory():
        buffer = torch.empty()
    triton_inplace_sin_cos_fused(buffer)
    return collective(buffer)
```


2) custom operator. Inductor just needs to run the custom operator underneath the symmetric memory context manager. The main risk of this is that more buffers than are needed get allocated with symmetric memory (all tensors produced by the custom op get allocated with symmetric memory), but the user can just re-write their custom op to optimize this

```py
requires_symmetric_memory(collective, input=0)

def user_code(x):
    y = custom_op(x)
    return collective(z)

def inductor_generated_code(x):
    with symmetric_memory():
        y = custom_op(x)
    return collective(y)
```

## What about eager-mode?

The API to specify which input needs symmetric memory only applies to torch.compile. So a user would end up writing code that looks like:
```py
requires_symmetric_memory(collective, input=0)

def user_code(x):
    if torch.compiler.is_compiling():
        with symmetric_memory():
            y = custom_op(x)
    else:
        y = custom_op(x)
    return collective(z)
```

## What is the API to specify which input needs symmetric memory?

@kwen2501 noted that the choice of which input needs symmetric memory is specific to the collective operator. So one design is just during operator registration, specify that the input needs symmetric memory.

1. torch.library.define("my_collective(SymmMemTensor x) -> Tensor")
2. torch.library.define("my_collective(Tensor x) -> Tensor", symm_mem_hint="x")

Another design is a torch.compiler API:

torch.compiler.specify_symmetric_memory(my_collective, "x").

If we think the choice is actually dynamic (or that some collectives may accept both symmetric and non-symmetric memory?) then this could instead be a context manager:
```py
@torch.compile
def user_code(y):
    x = custom_op(y)
    with torch.compiler.specify_symmetric_memory(my_collective, "x"):
        my_collective(x)
```

comments.author: Amir-19
comments.body:
- for option 1 (built-in operator), if the collective is not in-place, we also need to guarantee that the output is also allocated under the symmetric_memory ctx manager.
- for option 2  (custom operator), since all the allocations in the custom_op are going to use symmetric_memory, then we need to ensure that all participating ranks are going to maintain the symmetry. this can become a challenge and require further changes to the kernels--e.g. different ranks might works on different sizes of data.

more generally, option 1 can be quite useful for pure communication ops, but if we want arbitrary symm memory (for instance, in gemm+ar kernel the output and several barriers need to be allocated in symm memory), we still need to wrap the whole pattern and kernel call in a custom op.

comments.author: kwen2501
comments.body:
@nvcastet we are on the same page re eager design and UI.

Some clarification re compile discussion above:

1. We want to have the same user code no matter in eager or torch.compile mode.
That is, the user code looks what @nvcastet points out:
```
   with torch.cuda.use_mem_pool(symmetric_pool):
       y = foo(x)
   ....
   symmetric_op(y)
```

2. Given 1, it seems to me and @zou3519 that Dynamo would already hit the MemPool context, and thus should be able to leverage it as hint to Inductor codegen. For example, Dynamo can tag each output variable in the context region with a "symm" label. This may render the hints in the op's `m.def` somewhat redundant, other than cross checking. (Well, no entirely redundant in some cases, see 3).

3. The hints in `m.def` may not be entirely redundant because a user can "over-apply" a MemPool, for example:
```
   with torch.cuda.use_mem_pool(symmetric_pool):
       y = foo(x)
       z = bar(y)
   ....
   regular_op(y)
   symmetric_op(z)
```
With hints, it is possible for torch.compile to figure out that `y` does not actually need to be symmetric, thus shrinking the size of the symmetric MemPool. This can potentially have a positive effect that the default pool is kept big, thus not so easy to OOM.

4. While 3 is an add-on effect torch.compile can make, it is not essential to the enablement of torch.compile + symm MemPool. Thus we can leave it out for step 1 of this RFC, and defer the discussion of the hint format -- "SymmTensor" or "Tensor(&)" for example.

issues.title: [Inductor] Mix-Order Reduction: XBLOCK Derivation Ignores N in RMSNorm Backward, Causing Bandwidth Cliff
issues.author: liqiangxl
issues.body:
## Summary

The persistent-reduction RMSNorm backward kernel in Inductor derives `XBLOCK` solely from `RSPLIT_SIZE`, which itself scales with `M`. When `N` is large (e.g., 16384 for Llama-family models), increasing `M` drives `XBLOCK` up to 2 or 4—far too large for the register/cache footprint—and memory bandwidth drops to ~10% SOL. Auto tune `XBLOCK` recovers up to 4.4× on affected shapes.

## Workloads That May Hit This

For RMSNorm backward:

```
M = batch_size × sequence_length
N = hidden_size
```

Large `M` is routine in LLM training. Example with Llama-class `N = 16384` on GB200 (`num_sm = 152`):

| Workload | Batch | Seq Len | M | XBLOCK (main) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Single full-context sample | 1 | 131072 | 131072 | 2 |
| Two full-context samples | 2 | 131072 | 262144 | 4 |
| Large-batch 8K training | 32 | 8192 | 262144 | 4 |

These are multi-GB kernels, so the bandwidth cliff directly impacts training step time.

## Root Cause

Main's heuristic derives `XBLOCK` from `RSPLIT_SIZE`:

```python
RSPLIT_SIZE = clamp(floor_power_of_2(M / (8 * num_sm)), 16, 128)
XBLOCK = clamp(RSPLIT_SIZE // 32, min_x_block, 16)
```

For `N > 512`, this formula ignores `N` entirely. The result: larger `M` → larger `RSPLIT_SIZE` → larger `XBLOCK`. But the per-iteration load footprint scales as:

```
load_bytes ≈ num_load_stages × XBLOCK × N × element_size
```

With two load stages and a ~64 KiB target per iteration, the ideal relationship is:

```
XBLOCK × N ≈ 8192   (i.e., XBLOCK should shrink as N grows)
```

So for `N = 16384`, `XBLOCK` should be 1—not 2 or 4.

Concrete effect on GB200 with `N = 16384`:

| M | RSPLIT_SIZE | XBLOCK | Kernel Time | SOL |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32768 | 16 | 1 | 1038 µs | 39.1% |
| 131072 | 64 | 2 | 10946 µs | 14.9% |
| 262144 | 128 | 4 | 30967 µs | 10.5% |

Going from `M = 32K` to `M = 131K` (a 4× increase in work) results in a 10.5× increase in time because `XBLOCK` jumps from 1 to 2.

## Proposed Fix 

**Autotune XBLOCK candidates**

Add `XBLOCK ∈ {1, 2, 4}` as autotune candidates, constrained to:
- Power-of-two values
- `XBLOCK` divides `RSPLIT_SIZE`
- `NUM_STAGES` recomputed per candidate

## Benchmark Results

**Large N (the broken case):** XBLOCK autotune on clean main, `N = 16384`:

| M | Main | With XBLOCK Autotune | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32768 | 1038 µs | 1030 µs | 1.01× |
| 131072 | 10946 µs | 3459 µs | **3.16×** |
| 262144 | 30967 µs | 6991 µs | **4.43×** |

**Mid-range N (regression check):** `M = 131072`, confirming no harm:

| N | Main | With XBLOCK Autotune | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2048 | 250 µs | 253 µs | 0.99× |
| 4096 | 495 µs | 488 µs | 1.01× |
| 8192 | 960 µs | 961 µs | 1.00× |

The fix is neutral for moderate `N` and delivers large gains for `N ≥ 16384` at production `M` values.

issues.title: torch._inductor.config.combo_kernels = True` crashes inductor codegen with "Dynamic shape on reduction dimension is not supported"
issues.author: ad8e
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Claude repro:
```
"""
Minimal repro: `torch._inductor.config.combo_kernels = True` crashes inductor
codegen with "Dynamic shape on reduction dimension is not supported" when a combo
kernel groups a *persistent* reduction whose reduction dimension is dynamic.

Run:
    python combo_kernels_dynamic_reduction_repro.py

Expected: prints "OK". Actual: raises during compilation:

    File ".../torch/_inductor/codegen/triton_combo_kernel.py", line 550,
        in codegen_static_numels_sub_kernel
      raise RuntimeError(
    torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: RuntimeError: Dynamic shape on reduction dimension is not supported

Three conditions are jointly required (drop any one and it compiles fine):
  1. combo_kernels = True. The scheduler groups >= 2 independent compatible kernels
     into one ComboKernel (no foreach op needed). Here the two `.sum()`s are grouped.
  2. A *persistent* reduction. inductor's heuristic
     (torch/_inductor/codegen/choices.py: should_use_persistent_reduction) picks
     persistent for a small contiguous (ReductionHint.INNER) reduction. For a dynamic
     numel this branch is only taken when the symbol has a static upper bound <= the
     threshold (64); the torch._check(...) calls supply it. Both reductions need a
     bound -- an unbounded one falls back to a looped (non-persistent) reduction and
     the group no longer trips the assert.
  3. The reduction numel is symbolic (dynamic=True). A persistent reduction emits
     RBLOCK == rnumel as a tl.constexpr, but ComboKernel.codegen_static_numels_sub_kernel
     requires every sub-kernel's reduction numel to be a static int and raises otherwise.

  torch 2.12.0, torch.version.cuda 13.2, triton 3.7.0, NVIDIA B200 (sm_100), python 3.12

    # persistent reduction (statically_known_leq(numel, 64)).
    torch._check(a.shape[0] <= 32)
    torch._check(b.shape[0] <= 32)
    return a.sum(), b.sum()


def main():
    assert torch.cuda.is_available(), "needs a CUDA/Triton backend"
    a = torch.randn(16, device="cuda")
    b = torch.randn(16, device="cuda")
    print("OK", fn(a, b))


if __name__ == "__main__":

issues.author: shadow-orange41
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


When a function is compiled with `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` and called inside a `torch.autograd.forward_ad.dual_level()` context, the forward-mode AD tangent (JVP) is silently dropped — `unpack_dual(...).tangent` returns `None` instead of the expected tangent tensor.

The same function produces the correct tangent in eager mode and with the `cudagraphs` backend.

## Minimal reproduction

```python
import torch
import torch.autograd.forward_ad as fwAD

def fn(x):
    return (x ** 2).sum()

compiled_fn_inductor = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor")
compiled_fn_cudagraphs = torch.compile(fn, backend="cudagraphs")

x = torch.tensor([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
v = torch.ones(3)

with fwAD.dual_level():
    dual_input = fwAD.make_dual(x, v)
    out = compiled_fn_inductor(dual_input)
    jvp_inductor = fwAD.unpack_dual(out).tangent

with fwAD.dual_level():
    dual_input = fwAD.make_dual(x, v)
    out = compiled_fn_cudagraphs(dual_input)
    jvp_cudagraphs = fwAD.unpack_dual(out).tangent

with fwAD.dual_level():
    dual_input = fwAD.make_dual(x, v)
    out = fn(dual_input)
    jvp_eager = fwAD.unpack_dual(out).tangent

print("inductor compiled jvp:", jvp_inductor)
print("cudagraphs compiled jvp:", jvp_cudagraphs)
print("eager jvp:", jvp_eager)
```

issues.title: [compile] Handle shallow_copy_data_ device mutation in ProxyTensor instead of save/restore workaround
issues.author: mlazos
issues.body:
## Summary

During `make_fx` tracing and `FakeTensorProp`, in-graph `shallow_copy_data_` (used for cross-device `tensor.data = ...`) mutates the `fake_device` attribute on input FakeTensors. This requires a save/restore workaround in `graph_capture.py` and `compile_fx.py` to prevent the backend compiler from seeing incorrect input devices.

## Current workaround

We save `fake_device` on all FakeTensor args before `make_fx` / `FakeTensorProp`, then restore them after. See:
- `torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/graph_capture.py` (make_fx tracing)
- `torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py` (FakeTensorProp)

## Desired behavior

Handle `shallow_copy_data_` correctly in ProxyTensor, following how `t_()` works:

- ProxyTensor snapshots placeholder `meta["val"]` via `set_meta` -> `extract_val` -> `snapshot_fake` -> `fast_detach`, creating an independent FakeTensor copy
- The live FakeTensor gets mutated by the op, but the placeholder snapshot is unaffected
- `track_tensor_tree` updates the proxy slot to point at the mutation node

The snapshot mechanism should already protect placeholder metadata (sizes, strides, storage_offset) since `fast_detach` creates a new TensorImpl via `aten.detach`. However, `fake_device` is a Python attribute on the FakeTensor wrapper, not on the TensorImpl. The `fast_detach` path does capture `fake_device` at snapshot time (`FakeTensor(fake_mode, out, x.device)`), so placeholder snapshots should be independent.

The remaining issue is that the arg FakeTensors themselves are mutated and reused after `make_fx` returns. This may require either:
1. Confirming the snapshot mechanism is sufficient and removing the placeholder restoration (keeping only arg restoration)
2. Making `shallow_copy_data_`'s FakeTensor kernel not mutate in-place during tracing

Dynamo graph inputs may need a separate fix since they don't go through ProxyTensor's snapshot path.

issues.title: Inductor does not wait `AsyncCollectiveTensor` nested inside `DTensor._local_tensor`
issues.author: Lucaskabela
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

  ## Summary

AOT autograd's `process_inputs` scans `flat_args` for top-level `AsyncCollectiveTensor` (ACT) and records `act_input_indices` so the compiled graph's `inner_fn` can emit `args[i].trigger_wait()` before the kernel runs. 

This scan is non-recursive. When a DTensor carries an ACT in its `_local_tensor` slot (e.g., after `DTensor.redistribute(async_op=True)`, or from FSDP2's async all-gather), the ACT is invisible to `process_inputs`, no `trigger_wait()` is emitted, and the Inductor kernel executes on memory whose underlying collective may not have completed.

With `backend='eager'` the bug is masked because ACT's `__torch_dispatch__` (`torch/distributed/_functional_collectives.py:1080`) unwraps and waits inline on every op. Inductor bypasses `__torch_dispatch__` entirely.

## Minimal deterministic repro (single process)                                                                                          

  Shows the missing `wait_tensor` on a synthesized ACT — easy to run, proves the mechanism.

  ```python                                                                                                                                
  import os                                                       

  import torch
  import torch.distributed as dist
  import torch.distributed._functional_collectives as fc
  from torch.distributed._functional_collectives import AsyncCollectiveTensor                                                              
  from torch.distributed.device_mesh import init_device_mesh
  from torch.distributed.tensor import DTensor, Replicate                                                                                  
                                                                  
                                                                                                                                           
  def main() -> None:                                             
      os.environ.setdefault("RANK", "0")
      os.environ.setdefault("WORLD_SIZE", "1")                                                                                             
      os.environ.setdefault("MASTER_ADDR", "localhost")
      os.environ.setdefault("MASTER_PORT", "29550")                                                                                        
      dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=0, world_size=1)       
                                                                                                                                           
      wait_tensor_calls: list[str] = []                           
      orig_wait_tensor = fc.wait_tensor                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                           
      def counting_wait_tensor(t):
          wait_tensor_calls.append("wait_tensor")                                                                                          
          return orig_wait_tensor(t)                              

      fc.wait_tensor = counting_wait_tensor
                                                                                                                                           
      mesh = init_device_mesh("cpu", (1,))
                                                                                                                                           
      @torch.compile(backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)          
      def fn(x):                                                                                                                           
          return x + 1
                                                                                                                                           
      # Compile + warmup. The compile path goes through Python dispatch, which
      # does trigger_wait; clear the counter afterwards to isolate runtime.                                                                
      dt = DTensor.from_local(torch.randn(4, 4), mesh, [Replicate()])                                                                      
      dt._local_tensor = AsyncCollectiveTensor(dt._local_tensor.clone())                                                                   
      fn(dt)                                                                                                                               
      wait_tensor_calls.clear()                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                           
      # Pure runtime call with a fresh ACT.                       
      dt2 = DTensor.from_local(torch.randn(4, 4), mesh, [Replicate()])                                                                     
      dt2._local_tensor = AsyncCollectiveTensor(dt2._local_tensor.clone())                                                                 
                                                                                                                                           
      assert isinstance(dt2._local_tensor, AsyncCollectiveTensor)                                                                          
      assert dt2._local_tensor.completed is False                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                           
      _ = fn(dt2)
                                                                                                                                           
      print(f"wait_tensor calls during runtime: {len(wait_tensor_calls)}")
      print(f"ACT.completed after compiled call: {dt2._local_tensor.completed}")                                                           
                                                                                                                                           
      assert len(wait_tensor_calls) >= 1, (                                                                                                
          "BUG: Inductor ran the compiled kernel without calling wait_tensor "                                                             
          "on the nested AsyncCollectiveTensor."                  
      )                                                                                                                                    
                                                                  
      dist.destroy_process_group()                                                                                                         
                                                                  

  if __name__ == "__main__":
      main()
  ```

  **Output**:                                                                                                                              
  ```
  wait_tensor calls during runtime: 0                                                                                                      
  ACT.completed after compiled call: False                        
  AssertionError: BUG: Inductor ran the compiled kernel without calling wait_tensor...
  ```

  ## Multi-rank repro through public API (2 processes)

Reaches the same state organically via `DTensor.redistribute(async_op=True)` — no manual `_local_tensor` assignment. Uses gloo on CPU so no GPU/NCCL required; the missing `wait_tensor` is stream-agnostic, so CUDA/NCCL behaves the same.

  ```python
  import os

  import torch
  import torch.distributed as dist
  import torch.distributed._functional_collectives as fc
  import torch.multiprocessing as mp                                                                                                       
  from torch.distributed._functional_collectives import AsyncCollectiveTensor
  from torch.distributed.device_mesh import init_device_mesh                                                                               
  from torch.distributed.tensor import DTensor, Replicate, Shard                                                                           
  
                                                                                                                                           
  def worker(rank: int, world_size: int) -> None:                 
      os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"                                                                                              
      os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "29600"
      dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)                                                                    
                                                                                                                                           
      wait_calls: list[int] = []
      orig_wait_tensor = fc.wait_tensor                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                           
      def counting_wait_tensor(t):
          wait_calls.append(1)                                                                                                             
          return orig_wait_tensor(t)                              

      fc.wait_tensor = counting_wait_tensor
                                                                                                                                           
      mesh = init_device_mesh("cpu", (world_size,))
                                                                                                                                           
      local_shard = torch.arange(8.0).view(8, 1) + rank * 100.0   
      dt_sharded = DTensor.from_local(local_shard, mesh, [Shard(0)])
                                                                                                                                           
      # Shard -> Replicate is an all-gather. async_op=True preserves the ACT
      # on _local_tensor (see torch/distributed/tensor/_redistribute.py:1733).                                                             
      dt_replicated = dt_sharded.redistribute(                                                                                             
          placements=[Replicate()], async_op=True
      )                                                                                                                                    
                                                                  
      if rank == 0:                                                                                                                        
          print(                                                  
              f"dt_replicated._local_tensor type: "
              f"{type(dt_replicated._local_tensor).__name__}"
          )                                                                                                                                
  
      @torch.compile(backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)                                                                                   
      def fn(x):                                                  
          return x + 1.0

      # Warmup/compile — Python dispatch here triggers the wait.
      # Clear the counter to isolate the runtime path.                                                                                     
      _ = fn(dt_replicated)
      wait_calls.clear()                                                                                                                   
                                                                  
      dt_sharded_b = DTensor.from_local(local_shard.clone(), mesh, [Shard(0)])
      dt_replicated_b = dt_sharded_b.redistribute(                                                                                         
          placements=[Replicate()], async_op=True
      )                                                                                                                                    
                                                                  
      _ = fn(dt_replicated_b)                                                                                                              
                                                                  
      if rank == 0:
          print(f"\nRuntime wait_tensor calls (should be >= 1): {len(wait_calls)}")
          if len(wait_calls) == 0:                                                                                                         
              print("BUG confirmed via public API.")
                                                                                                                                           
      dist.destroy_process_group()                                


  def main():
      world_size = 2                                                                                                                       
      mp.spawn(worker, args=(world_size,), nprocs=world_size, join=True)
                                                                                                                                           
                                                                  
  if __name__ == "__main__":
      main()
  ```

**Output**:                                                                                                                              
  ```
  dt_replicated._local_tensor type: AsyncCollectiveTensor                                                                                  
                                                                  
  Runtime wait_tensor calls (should be >= 1): 0
  BUG confirmed via public API.
  ```

## Affected files
                                                                  
  - `torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/frontend_utils.py:73-77` — flat scan only.
  - `torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/subclass_codegen.py:269-271` — emits `args[i] = args[i].trigger_wait()` only for top-level indices.

## Likely fix
  1. `process_inputs`: recursively walk `__tensor_flatten__` on wrapper-subclass inputs and record ACT *paths* (e.g., `(i,                 
  "_local_tensor")`), not just flat indices.
  2. `subclass_codegen`: emit `args[i].<path> = args[i].<path>.trigger_wait()` for each recorded path, before subclass unwrapping runs.    

## Environment
                                                                                                                                           
  Reproduces on main (`bde493aade8`), CPU + gloo; stream-agnostic so CUDA/NCCL is equivalent.

## Correctness impact                                                                                                                    

Silent data corruption under real async collectives — the kernel reads a tensor whose collective is still in flight. The race often "wins" on localhost because collectives are fast, which is likely why this has gone uncaught. Most at risk: large tensors, slow interconnects (saturated PCIe / inter-node), contended GPUs.                                                                             
                                                                 

### Versions

  Reproduces on main (`bde493aade8`), CPU + gloo; stream-agnostic so CUDA/NCCL is equivalent.

issues.title: [Inductor] torch.compile loses signbit in torch.special.log_ndtr, causing discrepancies in sign-sensitive ops (e.g., copysign, atan2)
issues.author: xyt66665000
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug
When compiling `torch.special.log_ndtr` with the `inductor` backend, the output for large positive inputs (e.g., `x = 100.0`) evaluates to `0.0`, whereas eager mode evaluates to `-0.0`. 

While `-0.0` and `0.0` evaluate to `True` under `torch.allclose`, this difference in the signbit causes discrepancies in downstream operations that are sensitive to the sign of zero (such as `torch.copysign`, `torch.atan2`, etc.). For example, using `torch.copysign` on the output yields `-1.0` in eager mode, but `1.0` in compiled mode.

### Reproduce script
```python
import torch

print("torch:", torch.__version__)
print("cuda:", torch.version.cuda)

def fn(x):
    y = torch.special.log_ndtr(x)
    return torch.copysign(torch.tensor(1.0, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype), y)

x = torch.tensor([100.0], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

y_eager = fn(x)
y_compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)(x)
    
print("eager:", y_eager)
print("compiled:", y_compiled)
print("equal:", torch.equal(y_eager, y_compiled))
print("allclose:", torch.allclose(y_eager, y_compiled))
```

### Output logs
```text
torch: 2.14.0.dev20260612+cu130
cuda: 13.0
eager: tensor([-1.], device='cuda:0')
compiled: tensor([1.], device='cuda:0')
equal: False
allclose: False
```

### Root cause observation
The discrepancy originates from `torch.special.log_ndtr(x)` itself. If we only return `torch.special.log_ndtr(x)` for the same input, the outputs are:
* **Eager:** `tensor([-0.], device='cuda:0')`
* **Compiled:** `tensor([0.], device='cuda:0')`

issues.title: [Inductor][CPU] #180212 fix is incomplete — #178244 reproducer still fails identically on 2.12.0+cpu (workaround: assert_indirect_indexing=False)
issues.author: michalkrompiec
issues.body:
## TL;DR

PR #180212 ("[Inductor][CPP] Fix check_bounds for inductor cpp backend")
was marked as closing #178244 and landed in 2.12.0, but the original
reproducer from #178244 **still fails identically** on 2.12.0+cpu —
same generated CPP file, same source line, same column, same diagnostic.

**Workaround**: set `torch._inductor.config.assert_indirect_indexing = False`
BEFORE the first `torch.compile` call. This bypasses the broken bounds-check
codegen path entirely and the reproducer runs to completion.

The env var `TORCHINDUCTOR_DISABLE_CPP_BOUNDS_CHECK=1` does NOT work as a
workaround (still fails — kept here so others don't repeat the experiment).

## Tested versions

| Version    | Default config | `assert_indirect_indexing=False` |
|------------|----------------|----------------------------------|
| 2.11.0+cpu | FAILS          | (not tested, presumed works)     |
| 2.12.0+cpu | FAILS          | **PASSES** — all decode steps OK |

Both default-config failures emit at line 78, column 62 of the generated
`main.cpp`, on the `TORCH_CHECK` bounds-check for an indexed load in the
decode-step recompile:

```
main.cpp:78:62: error: 'tmp2' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'tm'?
```

## Reproducer

Identical to #178244. Copied here for self-contained reference:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def causal_fn(b, h, q, kv):
    return kv <= q


def padding_fn(padding_mask):
    def inner(b, h, q, kv):
        return padding_mask[b, kv]
    return inner


def and_masks(f1, f2):
    def combined(b, h, q, kv):
        return f1(b, h, q, kv) & f2(b, h, q, kv)
    return combined


def make_mask(batch_size, q_len, kv_len, q_offset, padding_mask):
    fn = and_masks(causal_fn, padding_fn(padding_mask))
    b = torch.arange(batch_size)[:, None, None, None]
    h = torch.arange(1)[None, :, None, None]
    q = (torch.arange(q_len) + q_offset)[None, None, :, None]
    kv = torch.arange(kv_len)[None, None, None, :]
    return fn(b, h, q, kv).expand(batch_size, 1, q_len, kv_len)


class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = torch.nn.Linear(32, 32, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, past_k, past_v, padding_mask, q_offset):
        B, S, _ = x.shape
        q = self.proj(x).view(B, S, 4, 8).transpose(1, 2)
        k = x.view(B, S, 4, 8).transpose(1, 2)
        v = k.clone()
        if past_k is not None:
            k = torch.cat([past_k, k], dim=2)
            v = torch.cat([past_v, v], dim=2)
        mask = make_mask(B, S, k.shape[2], q_offset, padding_mask)
        out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=mask)
        return out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, S, 32), k, v


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Uncomment to apply the workaround:
    # torch._inductor.config.assert_indirect_indexing = False

    print(f"torch {torch.__version__}")
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    compiled = torch.compile(Model().eval())
    pad = torch.ones(1, 8, dtype=torch.bool)
    pad[0, :2] = False
    with torch.no_grad():
        out, pk, pv = compiled(torch.randn(1, 8, 32), None, None, pad, 0)
        print("Prefill kv=8: OK")
        for step in range(3):
            pad = torch.cat([pad, torch.ones(1, 1, dtype=torch.bool)], dim=1)
            out, pk, pv = compiled(torch.randn(1, 1, 32), pk, pv, pad, pk.shape[2])
            print(f"Decode step {step + 1} kv={pk.shape[2]}: OK")
```

## Verification matrix

```
torch 2.12.0+cpu, default config:
  Prefill kv=8: OK
  Decode step 1: FAILED — InductorError: CppCompileError
  main.cpp:78:62: error: 'tmp2' was not declared in this scope

torch 2.12.0+cpu, assert_indirect_indexing=False:
  Prefill kv=8: OK
  Decode step 1 kv=9: OK
  Decode step 2 kv=10: OK
  Decode step 3 kv=11: OK
```

## Environment

- Platform: Linux x86_64, CPU only (gcc 13 system default)
- PyTorch: 2.11.0+cpu (FAILS) and 2.12.0+cpu (also FAILS)
- Python: 3.12

## Suggestion

Either re-open #178244 or treat this as a regression of the same code path
that #180212 attempted to fix. The bounds-check emit for closure-composed
mask + SDPA on CPU dynamic-shape recompile is the common root.

issues.title: torch.compile FX graph does not distinguish custom ops with the same name but different mutates_args
issues.author: efsotr
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

In `torch.compile`, changing only `mutates_args` of a custom op does not change its FX graph. As a result, custom ops with the same name but different `mutates_args` can hit the same Inductor cache entry.

This can cause incorrect behavior. For example, as shown in the code below, for a custom op that returns `None`, Inductor may eliminate the op when `mutates_args` is empty, but preserve it when `mutates_args` is non-empty. Since both versions share the same FX graph and cache key, a stale cached result can still be reused after `mutates_args` is corrected, unless the cache is manually cleared.


```python
# Test test_fx_graph_cache.py
# REMOVE_OLD_CACHE=1 python test_fx_graph_cache.py
# ADD_MUTATES_ARGS=1 python test_fx_graph_cache.py
# REMOVE_OLD_CACHE=1 ADD_MUTATES_ARGS=1 python test_fx_graph_cache.py

import os
import shutil
if os.environ.get("REMOVE_OLD_CACHE", "0") == "1":
    shutil.rmtree(f"/tmp/torchinductor_{os.environ.get('USER')}", ignore_errors=True)

import torch
from torch.library import Library, infer_schema  # noqa
from typing import Callable

test_lib = Library("test", "FRAGMENT")  # noqa

def direct_register_custom_op(
    op_name: str,
    op_func: Callable,
    mutates_args: list[str] | None = None,
    fake_impl: Callable | None = None,
    target_lib: Library | None = None,
    dispatch_key: str | None = None,
    tags: tuple[torch.Tag, ...] = (),
    schema_str: str | None = None,
):
    if mutates_args is None:
        mutates_args = []

    if dispatch_key is None:
        dispatch_key = "CUDA"

    if schema_str is None:
        schema_str = infer_schema(op_func, mutates_args=mutates_args)
    # print(f"Registering custom op '{op_name}' with schema: {schema_str} to library: {target_lib or test_lib}")

    my_lib = target_lib or test_lib
    my_lib.define(op_name + schema_str, tags=tags)
    my_lib.impl(op_name, op_func, dispatch_key=dispatch_key)
    if fake_impl is not None:
        my_lib._register_fake(op_name, fake_impl)


def create_output(shape, dtype, device):
    return torch.empty(shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)

def mul_out(x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor, *, out: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    torch.mul(torch.mul(x, y), x, out=out)

def fake_mul_out(x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor, *, out: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    return None

direct_register_custom_op(
    "mul",
    mul_out,
    mutates_args=["out"] if os.environ.get("ADD_MUTATES_ARGS", "0") == "1" else [],
    fake_impl=fake_mul_out,
    tags=(),
)


def mul_out_impl(x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor):
    out = create_output(x.shape, x.dtype, x.device)
    torch.ops.test.mul(x, y, out=out)
    return out

    y = torch.randn(4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

    s = torch.ones_like(x)
    del s
    out2_compiled = torch.compile(mul_out_impl)(x, y)
    print(out1.sum())
    print(out2_compiled.sum())

`mf` mask allows visual tokens to see future tokens (but not answer tokens):

```python
MOD_VISUAL = 0   # visual token
MOD_TEXT   = 1   # question text token
MOD_ANSWER = 2   # answer text token

def create_mf_mask(sample_id_map, modality_map):

        future_v2q = (q_idx < kv_idx) & q_is_visual & kv_is_question

comments.body:
Investigated on latest `main` (`2.13.0a0+git795be92`, CUDA H200) with my agent. Sharing runtime-traced findings that recharacterize the problem.

### Finding 1: `allow_rnn=True` works. dynamo traces LSTM/GRU successfully

With `torch._dynamo.config.allow_rnn = True`, dynamo bypasses the `builder.py` isinstance block and **successfully traces through** LSTM and GRU forward methods. The resulting FX graph keeps `aten.lstm` as a single op:

```
1-layer LSTM (h=5, seq=3):   12 FX nodes → compiled in 0.7s   [output matches eager (atol=1e-4)]
1-layer GRU  (h=5, seq=3):   compiled in 1.0s         [output matches eager (atol=1e-3)]
```

The compiled model's outputs match eager within normal float32 precision (~1e-4), and recompilation produces **exact bitwise matches**, confirming determinism.

### Finding 2: The reported "hang" is not in dynamo it's in inductor's `compile_fx`

For larger models, the issue isn't dynamo failing to trace — it's the inductor backend taking extremely long to lower the `aten.lstm` op. The FX graph stays small even for 6-layer LSTMs:

| Config | FX nodes | `compile_fx` time | Status |
|--------|----------|-------------------|--------|
| 1L, h=5, seq=3 | 12 | 0.7s | pass |
| 1L, h=64, seq=32 | 12 | 18.8s | pass |
| 2L, h=64, seq=16 | 16 | 5.6s | pass |
| 6L, h=256, seq=64 | **32** | **79.9s** | barely |
| 1L, h=256, seq=128 | 12 | >60s | timeout |
| 6L, h=256, seq=512 | 32 | >120s | timeout |

The FX graph for a 6-layer LSTM is only **32 nodes** (25 placeholders, 6 call_functions, 1 output), yet inductor's `compile_fx` spends 80 seconds. Timeout tracebacks consistently land in inductor subsystems: `scheduler.py:_can_fuse`, `pattern_matcher.py:_match`, and `graph.py:get_dep_size_hint`.

This is a separate inductor performance issue — the `aten.lstm` op's decomposition/lowering inside inductor produces a much larger internal graph that these passes struggle with.

### Finding 3: Without `fullgraph=True`, graph break recovery is broken

Related to #141184: when `allow_rnn=False` (default) and `fullgraph` is not set, dynamo graph-breaks on the LSTM but then **fails to compile any subgraph at all** — neither pre-LSTM nor post-LSTM. Dynamo emits:

```
empty checkpoint - cannot resume from graph break
Failed to handle graph break gracefully. Skipping the function and falling back to eager.
```

Result: 0 compiled graphs, the entire model runs in eager.

## Summary

There are actually **three distinct issues** here:
1. **Dynamo blocks RNN by default** (`allow_rnn=False`) — intentional, but the `allow_rnn=True` escape hatch works
2. **Graph break recovery is broken** (0 graphs compiled) — tracked at #141184
3. **Inductor `compile_fx` scales poorly** for `aten.lstm` lowering — 32-node FX graph takes 80s, making multi-layer/large LSTMs practically unusable. This seems to be the actual blocker and may warrant a separate inductor issue.

issues.title: [Inductor] int32 indexing selected for fused kernels whose address-constant offset exceeds 2**31, causing Triton compile error
issues.author: jia-wei-tang
issues.body:
[repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28544223/repro.py)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`SIMDKernelFeatures.select_index_dtype()` decides between `tl.int32` and
`tl.int64` based solely on `can_use_32bit_indexing(numel, buffers)`,
which inspects only

  * the kernel's total `numel`, and
  * each buffer's `storage_size`.

It does **not** inspect the indexing expressions themselves. After
fusion, indexing expressions of the form

    base + x0 + stride * x1

can carry a literal `base` (constant offset) whose magnitude exceeds the
int32 range `[-2**31, 2**31 - 1]`, even when every buffer's storage_size
fits in int32. Triton then refuses to compile the generated kernel with:

    ValueError: Scalar -2779057358 is out of range for type int32

A real-world trigger is `slice_scatter.backward` getting fused with an
`mm.backward` against a wide pooled embedding tensor — Inductor folds
all the slice ranges into per-load constant offsets, but the dtype
decision was already locked to int32.

### Versions

Pytorch 2.12.0 + cu130 (problem exists in all versions)

PyTorch version: 2.12.0+cu130

current main as of 2026-05), the backward pass crashes with:

    ValueError: Scalar -2779057358 is out of range for type int32

storage_size and total numel. But after fusion the address expression
becomes `base + x0 + stride*x1` where the literal `base` already exceeds
2**31. Triton refuses to compile this literal as int32.

Trigger pattern: multiple large 2-D tensors sliced at a high row offset,
concatenated on dim-1, then fed through per-column dense layers. The fused
backward kernel (slice_scatter + mm.backward) produces the oversized
constant.

  - PyTorch with CUDA support

import sys

import torch
from torch import nn

# (1) Each individual tensor's numel fits in int32.
# (2) The sliced working window fits in int32.
# (3) The fused address constant (SLICE_BEGIN * TOTAL_COLS) does NOT.

SLICE_BEGIN = 9_472_768
SLICE_END = 9_499_648
COL_WIDTHS = [32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 22]  # 10 groups, sum = 310
TOTAL_COLS = sum(COL_WIDTHS)
INT32_MAX = 2**31 - 1


def check_trigger_conditions():
    """Verify the three conditions that expose the bug."""
    # (1) Largest single buffer numel fits in int32
    assert TOTAL_ROWS * max(COL_WIDTHS) < INT32_MAX, "condition 1 violated"
    # (2) Sliced window numel fits in int32
    assert (SLICE_END - SLICE_BEGIN) * TOTAL_COLS < INT32_MAX, "condition 2 violated"
    # (3) Fused address constant overflows int32
    assert SLICE_BEGIN * TOTAL_COLS > INT32_MAX, "condition 3 violated"


class SliceConcatDense(nn.Module):
    """Slice each input at a high row offset, concat, apply per-group linears."""

    def __init__(self, widths):
        super().__init__()
        self.widths = widths
        self.linears = nn.ModuleList(
            [nn.Linear(w, w, bias=False) for w in widths]
        )

    def forward(self, inputs):
        sliced = [t[SLICE_BEGIN:SLICE_END, :] for t in inputs]
        cat = torch.cat(sliced, dim=1)  # [slice_rows, TOTAL_COLS]
        out = cat.new_zeros(())
        col = 0
        for w, linear in zip(self.widths, self.linears):
            out = out + linear(cat[:, col : col + w]).sum()
            col += w
        return out


def main():

        print("SKIP: CUDA not available", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    check_trigger_conditions()

    # Memory check: need ~2x leaf bytes (for .grad), with 1.3x safety margin
    leaf_bytes = sum(TOTAL_ROWS * w * 4 for w in COL_WIDTHS)
    need_gb = leaf_bytes * 2 / 1024**3 * 1.3
    free_gb = torch.cuda.mem_get_info()[0] / 1024**3
    if free_gb < need_gb:
        print(
            f"SKIP: need ~{need_gb:.1f} GiB free GPU memory, "
            f"have {free_gb:.1f} GiB",
            file=sys.stderr,
        )
        return 2

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    inputs = [
        torch.randn(TOTAL_ROWS, w, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
        for w in COL_WIDTHS
    ]
    model = SliceConcatDense(COL_WIDTHS).cuda()
    compiled = torch.compile(model, dynamic=False)

    try:
        loss = compiled(inputs)
        loss.backward()
    except ValueError as e:
        if "out of range for type int32" in str(e):
            print(f"BUG REPRODUCED: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
            return 1
        raise
    finally:
        del inputs, model, compiled
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    print("OK — no overflow (fix is effective)")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

This issue is in the tracer of dynamo. there is an inconsistent assignment for the sign of 0 of the real part of the complex tensor. 

This recreates OP's issue. 
```python
from torch.fx import Graph, GraphModule
# Define the constant complex tensor exactly as in your forward
const_x = torch.tensor([(-0 - 1e-28j)], dtype=torch.cfloat)

graph = Graph()
# Retrieve the constant by name

# Call the cosine method on it

# Return the result as a tuple to mirror your forward's (cos,)

# Build the GraphModule with the constant embedded

```

This does not have OP's issue
```python
from torch.fx import Graph, GraphModule
# Define the constant complex tensor exactly as in your forward
const_x = torch.tensor([(-1e-28j)], dtype=torch.cfloat)

graph = Graph()
# Retrieve the constant by name
x_node = graph.get_attr("const_x")
# Call the cosine method on it
cos_node = graph.call_method("cos", args=(x_node,))
# Return the result as a tuple to mirror your forward's (cos,)
graph.output((cos_node,))

# Build the GraphModule with the constant embedded
gm = GraphModule({"const_x": const_x}, graph, "CosineConstModule")

```

The key difference is that torch.tensor([(-1e-28j)], dtype=torch.cfloat) is traced as  torch.tensor([(-0-1e-28j)], dtype=torch.cfloat) in dynamo, which returns tensor([0.-1.0000e-28j]). ### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Description
When using `torch.compile` with the `inductor` backend, `torch.nextafter` produces incorrect results for non-contiguous `float16` tensors. 

Comparing eager mode and compiled mode, eager mode correctly computes the next representable floating-point value. However, the compiled function returns a tensor with the exact same bit pattern as the input tensor `x` (effectively doing nothing).

```python
import torch

print("torch:", torch.__version__)
print("cuda:", torch.version.cuda)

device = "cuda"
dtype = torch.float16

def fn(x, y):
    return torch.nextafter(x, y)

    [
        [-0.0, -1.0],
        [ 0.0,  2.0],
        [ 1.0, -2.0],
    ],
    device=device,
    dtype=dtype,
)

x = base.t()          
y = torch.zeros_like(x)

print("x:")
print(x)
print("x.is_contiguous():", x.is_contiguous())
print("x.stride():", x.stride())

y_eager = fn(x, y)

compiled_fn = torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)

print(y_eager)

print("\ncompiled:")
print(y_compiled)

print("\ntorch.equal:", torch.equal(y_eager, y_compiled))
print("torch.allclose:", torch.allclose(y_eager, y_compiled))

print("\neager bit pattern:")
print(y_eager.view(torch.int16))

print("\ncompiled bit pattern:")

issues.title: [CPU] `torch.compile` inductor C++ codegen fails when closure-composed mask functions are used with `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` across recompilations
issues.author: jiqing-feng
issues.body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

On **CPU**, when using `torch.compile` with a model that:

1. Builds an attention mask via **closure composition** (nested closures that capture a tensor and index it with broadcast indices)
2. Feeds the mask to `F.scaled_dot_product_attention`
3. Is called **multiple times with different input shapes** (triggering recompilation, e.g. prefill then decode in an autoregressive generation loop)

The inductor C++ codegen generates code that references an **undeclared variable** (e.g. `tmp2`), causing `g++` compilation to fail with `CppCompileError`.

**The same mask logic written inline (without closures) works fine.** The two approaches are mathematically equivalent — the only difference is whether the mask is constructed through composed closures or directly.

This bug was discovered in `transformers` ([huggingface/transformers#44458](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/44458)), where `masking_utils.py` uses exactly this closure composition pattern to build attention masks for all models.

## Key observation

| Mask construction | Result |
|---|---|
| Closure-composed: `and_masks(causal_fn, padding_fn(mask))` applied to broadcast indices | **FAILS** on recompilation |
| Inline equivalent: `mask[b, kv] & (kv <= q)` with same broadcast indices | Works fine |

This suggests dynamo traces the closure composition into a different FX graph structure than the inline equivalent, and inductor's C++ backend cannot correctly codegen for that specific graph on recompilation.

## Reproduction script

```python
"""
torch.compile inductor bug: closure-based mask + SDPA fails on recompilation (CPU only).

Same mask logic written inline works fine. Only the closure composition
pattern triggers a C++ codegen error (undeclared variable) on recompilation.
"""
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


# ---- Closure-based mask construction (triggers bug) ----

def causal_fn(b, h, q, kv):
    return kv <= q

def padding_fn(padding_mask):
    def inner(b, h, q, kv):
        return padding_mask[b, kv]
    return inner

def and_masks(f1, f2):
    def combined(b, h, q, kv):
        return f1(b, h, q, kv) & f2(b, h, q, kv)
    return combined

def make_mask_closure(batch_size, q_len, kv_len, q_offset, padding_mask):
    fn = and_masks(causal_fn, padding_fn(padding_mask))
    b = torch.arange(batch_size)[:, None, None, None]
    h = torch.arange(1)[None, :, None, None]
    q = (torch.arange(q_len) + q_offset)[None, None, :, None]
    kv = torch.arange(kv_len)[None, None, None, :]
    return fn(b, h, q, kv).expand(batch_size, 1, q_len, kv_len)


# ---- Inline mask construction (no closures, works fine) ----

def make_mask_inline(batch_size, q_len, kv_len, q_offset, padding_mask):
    b = torch.arange(batch_size)[:, None, None, None]
    kv = torch.arange(kv_len)[None, None, None, :]
    q = (torch.arange(q_len) + q_offset)[None, None, :, None]
    return (padding_mask[b, kv] & (kv <= q)).expand(batch_size, 1, q_len, kv_len)


# ---- Minimal model: mask + SDPA ----

class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, use_closure=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = torch.nn.Linear(32, 32, bias=False)
        self.use_closure = use_closure

    def forward(self, x, past_k, past_v, padding_mask, q_offset):
        B, S, _ = x.shape
        q = self.proj(x).view(B, S, 4, 8).transpose(1, 2)
        k = x.view(B, S, 4, 8).transpose(1, 2)
        v = k.clone()
        if past_k is not None:
            k = torch.cat([past_k, k], dim=2)
            v = torch.cat([past_v, v], dim=2)

        if self.use_closure:
            mask = make_mask_closure(B, S, k.shape[2], q_offset, padding_mask)
        else:
            mask = make_mask_inline(B, S, k.shape[2], q_offset, padding_mask)

        out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=mask)
        return out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, S, 32), k, v


# ---- Test: prefill then decode (shape changes → recompilation) ----

def test(label, use_closure):
    print(f"\n--- {label} ---")
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    model = Model(use_closure=use_closure).eval()
    compiled = torch.compile(model)

    pad_mask = torch.ones(1, 8, dtype=torch.bool)
    pad_mask[0, :2] = False  # 2 padding tokens

    # Prefill: seq_len=8
    x = torch.randn(1, 8, 32)
    with torch.no_grad():
        out, pk, pv = compiled(x, None, None, pad_mask, q_offset=0)
    print(f"  Prefill (kv=8): OK")

    # Decode steps: seq_len=1, kv grows each step → recompilation
    for step in range(3):
        pad_mask = torch.cat([pad_mask, torch.ones(1, 1, dtype=torch.bool)], dim=1)
        x = torch.randn(1, 1, 32)
        try:
            with torch.no_grad():
                out, pk, pv = compiled(x, pk, pv, pad_mask, q_offset=pk.shape[2])
            print(f"  Decode step {step+1} (kv={pk.shape[2]}): OK")
        except Exception as e:
            import traceback
            print(f"  Decode step {step+1}: FAILED — {type(e).__name__}")
            traceback.print_exc()
            return


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"torch {torch.__version__}")
    test("Closure-based mask (BUG)", use_closure=True)
    test("Inline mask (OK)", use_closure=False)
```

## Expected output

Both closure-based and inline tests should pass all decode steps, since they compute the same mask.

## Actual output (2.12.0.dev20260316+cpu / 2.10.0+cpu)

```
--- Closure-based mask (BUG) ---
  Prefill (kv=8): OK
  Decode step 1: FAILED — InductorError
  ...
  CppCompileError: C++ compile error
  ...
  error: 'tmp2' was not declared in this scope
  ...

--- Inline mask (OK) ---
  Prefill (kv=8): OK
  Decode step 1 (kv=9): OK
  Decode step 2 (kv=10): OK
  Decode step 3 (kv=11): OK
```

## Environment

- **Platform**: CPU only (tested on Linux x86_64)
- **PyTorch**: 2.12.0.dev20260316+cpu
- **Python**: 3.12
- **Compiler**: g++ (system default)

## Context

This pattern is used in HuggingFace `transformers` library's unified mask creation (`masking_utils.py`) which composes `causal_mask_function`, `padding_mask_function`, `sliding_window_mask_function`, etc. via `and_masks()` / `or_masks()`. This means **any model using `torch.compile` with padding tokens on CPU will hit this bug** (e.g. Mllama, Llama with padding, etc.).

Upstream issue: [huggingface/transformers#44458](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/44458)
Upstream workaround PR: [huggingface/transformers#44845](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/44845) (avoids closure composition for padding mask)

issues.title: benchmarks/dynamo/timm_models.py: model loading fails for models that don't accept drop_rate
issues.author: ashahba
issues.body:
### Problem description:
Running the timm benchmark with certain newer models (e.g. timm/gemma4_vit_570m_enc.gemma4_31b_it) fails at model load time with:
```
Gemma4VitEncoder.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'drop_rate'
```

### Reproduction
```
python \
    benchmarks/dynamo/timm_models.py --performance --inference --bfloat16 \
    --backend=inductor --output=timm_models_inference.csv --device xpu \
    --only timm/gemma4_vit_570m_enc.gemma4_31b_it
```
Or in isolation:
```
from timm.models import create_model
create_model(
    'timm/gemma4_vit_570m_enc.gemma4_31b_it', in_chans=3, scriptable=False,
    num_classes=None, drop_rate=0.0, drop_path_rate=None, drop_block_rate=None,
    pretrained=True,
)
```

### Root Cause
`_download_model` in `benchmarks/dynamo/timm_models.py` hardcodes `drop_rate`, `drop_path_rate`,
and `drop_block_rate` kwargs for all models. Newer timm model architectures (like Gemma4VitEncoder) do not accept these kwargs.

### Possible fix:
Retry `create_model` without the drop kwargs on TypeError:
```
@download_retry_decorator
def _download_model(self, model_name):
    try:
        model = create_model(
            model_name,
            in_chans=3, scriptable=False, num_classes=None,
            drop_rate=0.0, drop_path_rate=None, drop_block_rate=None,
            pretrained=True,
        )
    except TypeError:
        model = create_model(
            model_name,
            in_chans=3, scriptable=False, num_classes=None,
            pretrained=True,
        )
    return model
```
